newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italian CPI falls for fifth successive month.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italian CPI falls for fifth successive month.

text.p: Italian inflation fell for the fifth consecutive month in June, dipping to 1.4 percent year-on-year from 1.6 percent in May, national statistics office Istat said on Friday.
On a month-on-month basis, inflation remained unchanged.
Friday's data confirmed earlier preliminary figures from leading Italian cities and means the country's inflation rate is now at its lowest level since February 1969.
Istat said the inflation rate in the first six months of the year was 2.0 percent compared with the same period in 1996, while average inflation over the last 12 months was 2.5 percent.
However, the consumer price index looks set to climb again in the second half of the year for largely technical and statistical reasons.

The official inflation goal for 1997 as a whole is 2.5 percent but Italy's centre-left government has said the recent sharp slowdown means it will certainly come in under target, despite the forecast pick-up in price pressure.
Government, unions and business leaders welcomed the latest inflation data.

"This is an important and positive confirmation that inflation is falling and that it has reached useful levels to help...give stability to the economy," said Sergio Cofferati, head of the country's largest union, the Cigl.
Price growth has tailed off sharply over the past year, with inflation last June standing at 3.9 percent.
Economists say the fall has been largely due to depressed domestic demand, the high cost of credit with a stronger lira and a favourable trend in international commodity prices.
Istat said data last month showed a 0.4 percent month-on-month fall in entertainment and recreation costs, while food, furniture and teaching costs were flat.
Health and hotel costs each rose 0.2 percent month-on-month.
Recognising the decline in inflation, the Bank of Italy trimmed its official discount rate to 6.25 percent last Friday, a cut of 50 basis points.
It was the fourth time in less than 12 months that the central bank had reduced rates.
Analysts polled by Reuters earlier this week said they did not foresee more monetary easing until the autumn and the market barely moved on Friday's inflation data.
"It was already priced in," one bond trader in Milan said.

July's CPI figure will be helped by a government decision to reduce telephone and electricity tariffs this month but analysts said there would have to be an exceptional overall performance for the general inflation rate to fall again.
Inflation dipped 0.2 percent month-on-month in July 1996, meaning that even if consumer prices were unchanged this month, the annual rate would still edge higher.
